beta_new: Dramatic laybacking along a flake that opens leftward, followed by more flakes and some jamming, ends at a bolted anchor. A direct start via the neighbouring crack is possible.
Begin on the wall beside Humble's Tumble (on its right), work across the overlaps, then two bolts lead up and rightward; medium cams assist.
Begin in Crack of Dung, step out rightward to bolt one; four additional clips then take you along the arete.
Begin like Just Say No, veer right after roughly twenty feet, then continue directly upward by a pair of old bolts and across an overlap.
Face climbing leads by a bolt (the crux) into a broad crack and easier ground; if the crux defeats you, sidestep right from that bolt, surmount the little roof, and angle back left into the crack.
A corner crack opening rightward leads past a roof to the summit, optionally broken in half; the crux sits low in the corner partway up to the roof, and large cams protect the roof.
A steep wall full of holes. The opening is easy ground up to bolt one, and the upper part takes medium cams in the neighbouring crack on the left.
Steep, thin climbing with a sting; beyond the roof, keep to the left of the bolts.
A direct line straight up the middle of the face.

moves.from: little TCUs and supplementary cams are essential

value.text: Small TCUs and supplementary cams are essential.

beta_new: A rounded arete dividing the north face from the east, offering eight bolts of continuous friction and face moves.
Follow the sharp finger-width crack through huecos and multi-coloured rock; solid face holds and excellent protection arrive precisely when needed.

moves.from: Little cams, wires and slings are enough.

value.text: Small cams, nuts and slings are enough.

beta_new: A tough start in a thin crack, then past a roof with a bolt, then the superb hand crack above; an easy traverse rightward reaches the Pretty Face anchor, and the opening can be backed up with small cams.

Head for the big three-cornered roof, skirt it on its left, step back into the crack on the right and follow that to the top; another finish traverses leftward to the anchors above Something Sporting.
A lovely thin crack that curves up the wall, reached via a scramble over the face just beside the tree on its right.

First pitch: start with gear placed off someone's shoulders or from a stick, aid until it goes free, then trace the crack leftward and up to the fixed belay.

Second pitch: traverse rightward under the big roof until you balance on an iron flake the size of a plate, then crank the obvious roof-capped dihedral crack.

moves.from: carry varied natural protection, including TCUs

beta_new: Follow the splitter hand-to-fist crack to its bulging exit moves, then finish by the large cedar tree.
Layback the large flake to the horn on top and then trend rightward to finish.

moves.from: protection is a small nut and a mid-size cam

beta_new: Follow the line with a central crack; it drifts right near the top, and finishing straight up is the harder variation.

moves.from: Mixed protection: two quickdraws and a mid-size piece.

value.text: Two quickdraws and one mid-size piece.

beta_new: Follow the clear-cut dihedral crack at the hallway's main corner; protection is mixed (varied sizes plus a bolt), and wires work nicely high up.
Shuffle rightward along the roof edge to the arete, then ascend directly to the ledge using small natural gear.
Inhale to stick, exhale and gain an inch, and repeat; it has seen a number of lead ascents since, one using wooden blocks for protection.
Start by the tree, just beyond So Low, and climb in much the same vertical edging style as that neighbor.
Leave the old chains with a hard pull off a sloping ledge onto easier ground, then pull a committing deadpoint from two crimps to the top-out jug. Two extra bolts go in beyond Flour Power.

Start by a small rhododendron and get through a blank-looking low section, then angle up and left to the prominent right-facing corner. Follow that dihedral to its end and continue over the pocketed wall and on to the chains.
Opening bolts one through three sit on dirty, fragile rock; once past them, everything above improves somewhat.
Start at the right side and work leftward, passing a vintage piton plus three bolts that spin, to reach the top.

moves.from: Descend by walking off to the right.

beta_new: Trend up and to the left across the slab toward the shared anchors.

Go up the flake until the first bolt is clipped, move rightward and make one hard pull onto a jug. Shake out there and drift back slightly left.

Above, big moves on the overhanging face lead to a difficult finish using edges and gastons.
Follow the wide crack set in a shallow, narrow dihedral, stemming and grinding upward.

The start is mossy, but the crack gets better quickly as you go up.

Large cams are handy for building the belay at the ledge.

moves.from: Large cams are handy for building the belay at the ledge.

beta_new: The crux comes low and has bolt protection, and you top out onto the ledge above.
Pass through the overhanging lower part to reach a blank face; work out that section, after which larger holds lead the rest of the way to the anchors.
Start from the ramp that a big boulder forms, pick the correct pockets through the steep part, then cruise up bigger holds until you reach the anchors.
Positive holds lead to the intimidating roof, which is marked by a fixed draw. Locate the crucial holds, cut your feet loose, and fight the barn-door swing, then hold on until the chains.
Locate the pedestal, then follow the face on its left, clipping bolts up to anchors beneath the bulge.
The face leans out a bit and has a pair of cruxes; a hands-free rest lies off to the left if wanted. A steep flake near the top gets very pumpy before the chains.

Pitch one: go up the ramp to a big ledge and belay from bolts.

Pitch two: go right via a hallway toward the next start, climb the dihedral that faces right until a hand-sized ledge, shuffle along that ledge into a fist crack angling right, and follow it to the top.
A tight corner with a few overhanging steps along the way, ending at a tree anchor.

Head for the roof roughly twenty feet off the ground, then shift leftward and upward into the dihedral.

Stem the dihedral through an obvious thin crux into a wide crack, which goes on to the ledge; two very large cams help with that wide part.
Start from the big boulders at the base, latch the arete and ride it until it becomes a narrow crack, which carries on to the anchors.
